comments.author: @leechumbley5440
comments.text: Very interesting to see Nusaybin, which played an important role in the transfer of Greek science to the Arabs. Really enjoyed the pictures of Diyarbakir and its oral bards. To see the Zogra villages was fascinating. And of course the amazing Citadel of Sulaemaniya. The Ishak Bey palace was remarkable. None of the 4 countries (Turkey, Syria, Iraq, Iran) fully accepts its Kurdish citizens. Kurdish is an Indo-European language like Persian, unlike Arabic (Semitic) and Turkish (Altaic). The WWI victors at the Treaty of Versailles promised the Kurds autonomy, but it never came to fruition. As you moved across the various regions, the continuity was apparent. I don't know of anyone else who has shown ethnic (rather than as defined by political borders) Kurdistan as a contiguous whole.

replies.author: @PlanetVista4K
replies.text: Thank you for your thoughtful insights and for watching our documentary on Kurdistan! 🙏

replies.text: You're absolutely right to point out that there are many ethnic groups without a country of their own, and the Uyghurs are indeed a very prominent example. comments.text: Structures like the 6,000-year-old Citadel of Erbil or the terraced village of Palangan are architectural masterpieces. But will commercialization and tourism development in these remote areas actually help preserve the traditional Kurdish way of life, or will it erode their true authenticity?

replies.author: @PlanetVista4K
replies.text: That's a really insightful question about the delicate balance between preservation and progress. It's a challenge many historical sites face, and finding that sweet spot is crucial.
